en: In formulas, the average when all friend lists are joined together and one name is drawn is <k²>/<k>, which is at least the average <k> (larger unless everyone has the same number of friends). The cards on this page instead compute each person's "friends' average" and average those, which is also always at least the average friend count because each friendship contributes (neighbour's friends ÷ my friends) + (my friends ÷ neighbour's friends) ≥ 2. Over 300 default networks the two values were 10.17 and 9.70, both larger than 5.92.

The sampling in the animation draws "a friend named by a randomly chosen person", so it converges to the average of per-person friend averages (10.17). Christakis and Fowler (2010), "Social network sensors for early detection of contagious outbreaks", PLoS ONE 5(9), proposed using this property: comparing randomly chosen Harvard students with the friends they named, they reported that the flu outbreak appeared earlier in the friend group. That was a proposal tested in one university sample, and this page does not reproduce it.
The layout is precomputed with a force-directed algorithm (Fruchterman-Reingold) where neighbours attract and everyone repels. You can verify with node tools/validate-friendship.js.
The code is available on GitHub.
Why Does the Bus Always Make You Wait Longer? · Simulatio Lab

If a bus comes every 10 minutes on average, why can you end up waiting 10 minutes on average? Run the waiting-time paradox (inspection paradox) and see why your class always feels more crowded than average.

"The bus is supposed to come every 10 minutes on average, so why do I always wait longer?" With a 10-minute average gap, showing up at a random moment should mean waiting 5 minutes on average. But if buses arrive unevenly, the average wait can be 10 minutes, not 5. It is not bad luck: a person who arrives at a random moment is more likely to land inside a long gap. Change how uneven the buses are, the average gap and the number of passengers, then check whether the same illusion explains why your class feels more crowded than the school average.

Buses come every average gap minutes, but the real gaps vary according to a gamma distribution. An irregularity (coefficient of variation = standard deviation of the gap ÷ mean) of 0 means a strict timetable, 1 means random arrivals, and larger values mean buses arrive in bunches.
Passengers do not know the timetable and arrive at any moment. The time until the next bus is the wait, and the bus gap they happened to land in is the gap the passenger saw.

A long gap takes up more room on the time axis, so the chance of a passenger landing in it is proportional to its length. That makes the average gap passengers see larger than the average gap you get by counting buses. The theory: average wait = average gap ÷ 2 × (1 + CV²).

The last panel applies the same calculation to class sizes. Counting classes one by one gives an average of 25, but if you ask students "how many are in your class?", students from big classes answer more often, so the average grows.

① Passengers Arrive One by One

Each time a passenger arrives, you see the bus gap they landed in (orange) and their wait (red line). The blue dots are earlier passengers, and far more of them sit inside long gaps. The line below is the average wait so far.
② Gaps Counted by Bus vs Gaps Seen by Passengers

The blue bars are the distribution of gaps when you count buses one by one, and the orange line is the distribution of the gaps passengers actually landed in. The orange one leans toward long gaps, which pushes its mean to the right.

③ The More Uneven, the Longer the Wait

The horizontal axis is how uneven the buses are and the vertical axis is the average wait. Blue is measured, the gold line is the theory (average gap ÷ 2 × (1 + CV²)), and the gray dashed line is the naive "half the gap" estimate. They match only at the far left, where buses run on a strict timetable.

④ The Same Illusion: Why Is My Class Always Crowded?

We create 1,000 classes with an average of 25 students (the unevenness is set by the slider above) and compare the average counted class by class with the average you get by asking each student the size of their own class. Big classes hold more students, so "big class" answers pile up.
Class sizes (counted class by class)
Own class size reported by students

What it shows: With a 10-minute average gap and random arrivals (irregularity 1.0), counting buses gave an average gap of 10.1 minutes, but the average gap passengers saw was 20.2 minutes (theory 20.0), and the average wait was 10.1 minutes (theory 10.0), twice the naive 5 minutes (20,000 buses, 40,000 passengers). On a strict timetable (0) the average wait was 5.0 minutes, equal to the naive estimate; it was 6.3 minutes at 0.5 (theory 6.3) and grew to 25.0 minutes at 2.0 (theory 25.0). In the default setting (500 passengers), only 13% of bus gaps were 20 minutes or longer, yet 41% of passengers landed in such a gap. The median wait was 7.0 minutes, but the longest wait was 60.7 minutes. Class sizes follow the same arithmetic. With 20,000 classes averaging 25 students, an unevenness of 0.3 gave a class average of 25.0 and a student-experienced average of 27.3 (theory 27.3); at 1.0 it was 49.8 (theory 50.0). Your class feels more crowded than average not by imagination but because big classes contain more students.

What it doesn't show: This does not mean most real buses are this uneven. The model is a simple one in which gaps are independent, and an irregularity of 1.0 was chosen to show "random arrivals", not measured on a real route. On timetabled routes people time their arrival to the schedule, so "arriving at any moment" does not hold and waits can be much shorter (this model fits frequent service where people go out without checking the timetable). It does not explain the psychological effect that unpleasant memories last longer either. In the class panel, sizes are rounded to integers of at least 1, so above an irregularity of 1.5 the results drift from the theory a little (82.5 vs 81.3 at 1.5). This project has not measured how uneven real classes are, and the 0.3 used as "realistic" is just an example value. For large values such as 2, rare long gaps dominate the average, so even 3,000 passengers can land away from the theory.
